The Great knot (Calidris tenuirostris) is a large-bodied migratory shorebird with a strongly structured life cycle shaped by its high-latitude breeding grounds and extensive intercontinental movements. At hatching from the incubated egg, which typically occurs at an external temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], the downy chick emerges with an initial wet weight of approximately 22 grams [Ww0 = approximately 22 grams], a modest mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to a precocial hatchling. This neonatal body size is consistent with that of other Calidris species and represents the starting point for a rapid period of somatic growth during the brief Arctic summer. The incubation period itself lasts around 22 days [ab = around 22 days] at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a duration that falls within the typical range of 21 to 23 days observed in field studies of this species. The relatively short incubation period is an adaptation to the compressed breeding window of the tundra, where thermal conditions and insect availability dictate a tight schedule for nesting success and chick development.

After hatching, the nestling chick begins a phase of rapid mass increase, driven by intensive parental provisioning of invertebrate prey. The fledgling period marks a critical developmental milestone, occurring at approximately 18 days after birth [tx = approximately 18 days after birth] under the ambient temperatures typical of the breeding grounds, which average around 41 °C [T = 41 °C] during peak summer activity. This age at fledging, which can range from 18 to 20 days, represents the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and gains a degree of independence from its parents. The attainment of flight capability at this early age is an evolutionary imperative, allowing juveniles to begin the demanding migratory journey southward before the onset of severe Arctic weather. This fledging period is relatively compressed compared to that of many temperate-breeding shorebirds, reflecting the intense time constraints imposed by the high-latitude environment.

Following the fledgling phase, the immature bird enters a protracted juvenile period dedicated to migration, foraging, and somatic growth. Puberty, the stage at which gonadal maturation is completed, is reached at approximately 150 days after birth [tp = approximately 150 days after birth] when individuals are exposed to the standard metabolic conditions of 41 °C [T = 41 °C] that characterize their active thermoregulatory state. This timing of sexual maturation is relatively late for a shorebird of this body size, likely a consequence of the substantial energetic investment required for the first long-distance migration and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support future reproductive effort. The juvenile bird must attain an adequate body condition before the onset of breeding, with the ultimate wet weight for males reaching 156 grams [Wwi = 156 grams] and for females a somewhat higher 174 grams [Wwi = 174 grams], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is common among migratory waders.

The first successful breeding event, representing the age at first reproduction, is a crucial demographic parameter. Field observations indicate that Great knots delay breeding until they have acquired full adult plumage and sufficient body condition, with the time since birth at the first brood equating to 730 days [tR = 730 days] under warm active temperatures of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This two-year delay before initial reproduction is characteristic of long-lived shorebirds and is thought to reflect the time needed to master complex migratory routes, secure high-quality foraging territories, and develop the physiological capacity for egg production. Females lay a single clutch of eggs annually [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs annually], an abbreviated reproductive output that is typical of Arctic-breeding scolopacids constrained by a short season. The trade-off between current reproductive investment and adult survival is thus clearly evident in this species.

Longevity data for the Great knot indicate a maximum lifespan on the order of 27.3 years [am = 27.3 years], a value documented from long-term recapture studies of color-banded individuals under the standard temperature conditions of 41 °C [T = 41 °C] that define their active metabolic environment. This substantial lifespan places the species among the longer-lived members of the Scolopacidae and is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by low annual fecundity, deferred maturity, and high adult survival.
